newsitem.title: FINLAND: ANALYSTS STILL SEE UPSIDE IN FINNLINES .
newsitem.headline: ANALYSTS STILL SEE UPSIDE IN FINNLINES .

text.p: Higher earnings and chances for benefits from cooperation would justify a higher valuation for Finnish cargo shipping firm Finnlines Oy, analysts said on Wednesday.
Though the shares have gained some 50 percent this year, buy recommendations for Finnlines shares are still maintained.
"Finnlines is not yet too expensive, we still recommend to buy it," said Aktia Bank analyst Ritva Ojala.
Finnlines' rising trend accelerated in early October and the shares have added over 10 percent in just two weeks.
Domestic and overseas demand has been fuelled by a sharp increase in Jan-Aug profits -- and by its option to up its stake in Swedish BTL which added speculative interest, analysts said.
"The valuation of Finnlines' business has been low, and now the option in BTL gives an additional lever for the stock," said Merita transport analyst Tanja Lounevirta.
"We still have a positive view on the stock," she added.
Finnlines on September 27 reported eight-month profits after financial items jumping to 302 million markka from 202 million.
On October 7, it said it had an option to up its ownership in Swedish transport group Bilspedition Transport & Logistics AB (BTL) to 45 percent of votes from 25 percent.

Although BTL said it did not expect a bid from Finnlines -- whose comments about its intentions with the options have been muted -- there are now hopes that links between the two would bring benefits to Finnlines, strengthening it on the Baltic market also in land transport.

Finnlines rose 3.30 markka on Wednesday to set a new year-high at 109.50 markka, which Ojala said is about seven times her forecasts for the company's 1996 earnings and about eight times 1997 earnings.
The Helsinki stock exchange is now trading at over 10 times forecast 1996 earnings, she said.
Analysts said owning a stake in BTL would be beneficial for Finnlines even without closer ties, since its profit is expected to rise further after recovering in 1995 from a 1994 loss.
Ojala said this could boost Finnlines' profits, which she expected to ease in 1997 after a sharp rise in 1996 after it sold its Huolintakeskus unit earlier this year.
